summary: This clipped AllThingsNature article by Kat Yares, last modified March 5, 2024, explains that thunder comes from the rapid expansion of air heated by a lightning bolt, which creates an acoustic shock wave. It covers how distance, bolt shape, and nighttime temperature inversions affect how thunder sounds, outlines early mistaken explanations, and answers common FAQs such as whether thunder can occur without lightning and how far thunder can be heard. Much of the page is comment threads and site navigation, which were ignored.
one_line: Explains that thunder is the acoustic shock wave from superheated air expanding along a lightning bolt's path, plus related FAQs.
key_facts: Thunder is caused by the sudden expansion of the air around a lightning bolt's path.
The air around a lightning bolt is superheated to up to about 54,000° Fahrenheit (about 33,000° Celsius).
A lightning strike takes just a few thousandths of a second to go from the clouds to the ground and back up along the same pathway.
The electrostatic discharge heats the surrounding air to a temperature roughly five times hotter than the surface of the sun.
The heated air becomes compressed to many times the normal atmospheric pressure because it does not have time to expand.
A nearby lightning strike sounds like a loud crack or snap, while distant lightning sounds more like a long rumble.
Thunder sounds louder at night because cold air near the ground and warmer air higher up, called an inversion, trap acoustic shock waves.
Before the 20th century, science could not explain thunder, and early Greeks believed it was caused by clouds colliding.
Thor, a god of Norse mythology, is named for the Old Norse word for thunder and is usually portrayed wielding a thunder-clapping hammer.
According to the National Severe Storms Laboratory, every instance of thunder is accompanied by lightning, although the lightning may not be seen.
Light travels at 299,792 kilometers per second, while sound travels at about 343 meters per second, which causes the delay between seeing lightning and hearing thunder.
Thunder can typically be heard up to 10 miles (16 kilometers) from the lightning strike under ideal conditions.
Every five seconds between the flash and the bang represents approximately one mile of distance to the storm.
Thundersnow occurs when there is strong enough instability and moisture in the atmosphere, typically near a strong low-pressure system.
